etymologies.etymologyHTML: Recorded since c.1205 as Middle English cable, from Old Northern French cable, from Late Latin capulum (“lasso, rope, halter”), from Latin capiō (“to take, seize”). Use of the term "cable" to refer to the USD/GBP exchange rate originated in the mid-19th century, when the exchange rate began to be transmitted across the Atlantic by a submarine communications cable.

definitions.definition: A strong, large-diameter wire or rope, or something resembling such a rope.
An assembly of two or more cable-laid ropes.
An assembly of two or more wires, used for electrical power or data circuits; one or more and/or the whole may be insulated.
(nautical) A strong rope or chain used to moor or anchor a ship.

quote.citation: 1851 November 14, Herman Melville, chapter 9, in Moby-Dick; or, The Whale, 1st American edition, New York, N.Y.: Harper & Brothers; London: Richard Bentley, →OCLC:
quote.text: “And now the time of tide has come; the ship casts off her cables; and from the deserted wharf the uncheered ship for Tarshish, all careening, glides to sea.

definitions.definition: (material) A long object used to make a physical connection.
(television) Ellipsis of cable television, broadcast over the above network, not by antenna.
(communication) A system for transmitting television or Internet services over a network of coaxial or fibreoptic cables.

quote.citation: 2014 March 15, “Turn it off”, in The Economist‎[1], volume 410, number 8878:
quote.text: If the takeover is approved, Comcast would control 20 of the top 25 cable markets,  […] . Antitrust officials will need to consider Comcast’s status as a monopsony (a buyer with disproportionate power), when it comes to negotiations with programmers, whose channels it pays to carry.

definitions.definition: A telegram, notably when sent by (submarine) telegraph cable.
(nautical) A unit of length equal to one tenth of a nautical mile.
(unit, chiefly nautical) 100 fathoms, 600 imperial feet, approximately 185 m.
(finance) The currency pair British Pound against United States Dollar.
(architecture) A moulding, shaft of a column, or any other member of convex, rounded section, made to resemble the spiral twist of a rope.
(knitting) A textural pattern achieved by passing groups of stitches over one another.
(transitive) To provide with cable(s)
(transitive) To fasten (as if) with cable(s)
(transitive) To wrap wires to form a cable
(transitive) To send a telegram, news, etc., by cable

quote.citation: 1946, George Johnston, Skyscrapers in the Mist, page 89:
quote.text: Details of a bottle fight in El Morocco were cabled all over the world.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To communicate by cable
(architecture, transitive) To ornament with cabling.
(knitting) To create cable stitches.

quote.citation: 2008, Leisure Arts, I Can't Believe I'm Knitting Cables, page 9:
quote.text: You've been cabling, twisting, popcorning and bobbling. See, we told you that they weren't so hard.
